title: An evaluation of estimative uncertainty in large language models
abstract: Words of estimative probability (WEPs), such as “maybe” or “probably not” are ubiquitous in natural language for communicating estimative uncertainty. In linguistics, WEPs are hypothesized to have special (probabilistic) semantics, and their calibration with numerical estimates has long been an area of study. Motivated by increasing usage of large language models (LLMs) in applications requiring robust communication of uncertainty, this article studies how divergences in interpreting WEP between humans and LLMs reveal the limits of statistical language models in reproducing the subtleties of communication under uncertainty. Through a detailed empirical study, we show that established LLMs align with human estimates from an established (Fagen–Ulmschneider) survey only for some WEPs presented in English. Divergence is also observed for prompts using gendered and Chinese contexts. Upon further investigating the ability of GPT-4 to consistently map statistical expressions of uncertainty to appropriate WEPs, we observe significant performance gaps. The results contribute to a growing body of research on using LLMs to study complex communicative phenomena under diverse experimental conditions.

claims.text: GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 probability distributions diverge significantly from human survey distributions for 13 out of 17 WEPs presented in concise English contexts.
Human and GPT probability distributions are statistically indistinguishable for high-certainty WEPs such as 'almost certain' and 'almost no chance'.
GPT-3.5 consistently exhibits lower divergence from human WEP estimates than GPT-4 across most contextual analyses.
GPT probability distributions under gender-specific narrative contexts exhibit lower variability compared to human distributions, with several WEP distributions collapsing into a single point.
ERNIE-4.0 probability distributions show low KL divergence compared to human distributions for 16 WEPs, but display statistically significant Brunner-Munzel test differences for 10 WEPs.
Chain-of-Thought prompting significantly improves GPT-4's performance only when evaluated using empirical consistency.
GPT-4 achieves significantly higher pair-wise consistency when provided with five WEP choices compared to three WEP choices.
GPT-4 achieves higher empirical consistency and empirical monotonicity consistency when provided with three WEP choices compared to five WEP choices.

limitations.text: The reference human uncertainty estimates were obtained from a single online survey with 123 participants, which may not be fully representative of the broader population's understanding of WEPs.
Elicited numeric probability outputs from LLMs are sensitive to prompting templates and decoding parameters, representing output-level behavior rather than internal belief states.
The evaluation of GPT-4's mapping from statistical uncertainty to WEPs relies on artificially generated data scenarios rather than complex real-world data.
The study only evaluated 17 specific WEPs present in the Fagen-Ulmschneider survey rather than a broader spectrum of probabilistic expressions.
The evaluation focused on static prompts and did not examine dynamic adjustments of probability estimations during multi-turn interactive conversations.

future_work.text: Survey a broader and more diverse demographic population using robust probability elicitation techniques to validate human WEP baseline estimates.
Evaluate LLM performance in mapping statistical uncertainty to WEPs using real-world scenarios and empirical statistical data from scientific publications.
Conduct cross-linguistic uncertainty estimation studies covering a broader set of languages using formal linguistic equivalence testing.
Examine how LLMs dynamically update and adjust their WEP probability estimations in response to evolving contexts within interactive dialogue.
Investigate whether human listeners attribute similar levels of confidence and credibility to estimative uncertainty statements generated by AI models compared to humans.

methodologies.name: WEP Probability Elicitation Benchmarking
methodologies.description: Elicits numerical probability estimates for 17 WEPs from language models across four narrative context settings and two languages, comparing elicited distributions to human survey data using KL divergence and Brunner-Munzel tests.

methodologies.name: Statistical Uncertainty to WEP Consistency Evaluation
methodologies.description: Evaluates GPT-4's ability to consistently select appropriate WEPs when presented with numerical sample data across three scenarios using four custom consistency metrics under standard and Chain-of-Thought prompting.
